catalog_citation: Sawada, Hideo. 1999. Outline of Phonology of Lhaovo (Maru) of Kachin State. In: Linguistic & Anthropological Study on the Shan Culture Area. Tokyo: ILCAA, pp. 97-147 (author's PDF at https://www.aa.tufs.ac.jp/~sawadah/works/).

catalog_quote: The syllable structure of Lhaovo is: (C)V(F)/GT ... G = Glottalizedness Feature[±Glottalized] ... T = Toneme ... Lhaovo has three tonemes: Falling(F) 21; Sometimes 32 in word-initial position followed by another F; 31 after L. Low(L) 22–33; Always 22 in word-initial position followed by F; the end of the syllable rises a little bit before another L. High(H) Syllables with final stop: 44; 42 in either it has a diphtong, or it is in word-initial position. ... loF “to come back” loL “anymore” loH “to go back” ... Syllables with final stop, as well as others, show three-term opposition for tone. ... 9.1 Syllable Weakening. All syllables in Lhaovo are not “full” syllable. Some syllable are “weak” ones, that is, syllables without inherent toneme. A weak syllable depends on the syllable immediately following it, therefore it cannot appear in word/phrase final position. audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at all three locators in the held author's-PDF of Sawada 1999, a dedicated 51-pp fieldwork phonology by the language's main specialist; the paper has an obligatory Toneme slot in the syllable template, three tonemes with minimal triplets on open and checked syllables, and toneless weak syllables, and contains no stress/accent statement, so kind=tonal with empty rule and domain UNSTATED is correct. Okell 1988 (fetched sources now, open CC BY-SA) independently gives a 3-tone (2 on checked) system with no stress mention, and the held Sawada 2018 Lhangsu phonology likewise has tones + weak syllables and zero stress/accent hits. The only larger description (Dai 2005, Chinese, print-only) covers the PRC variety and is not expected to alter a tonal coding.

sources.citation: Okell, John A. 1988 [online ed. dated 1989]. Notes on tone alternation in Maru verbs. In D. Bradley, E.J.A. Henderson & M. Mazaudon (eds), Prosodic analysis and Asian linguistics: to honour R.K. Sprigg, 109-114. Pacific Linguistics C-104. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C104.109 (CC BY-SA online edition via sealang.net).
sources.quote: 'Tones in Maru are engagingly straightforward: there are three tones (high, mid and low) in unchecked syllables ... and two tones (high and low) in checked syllables' (p.110); the rest documents a regular morpheme-conditioned one-step tone raising in verbs. No mention of stress or accent anywhere (grep stress|accent: 0 hits); negative/nominalizer prefixes are discussed only for their (non-)effect on tone raising.
sources.locator: sec. 1 'Tone in Maru', p.110; secs. 2-3 pp.110-114
